source.title: Recent Theoretical Advances and Open Problems in Nuclear Cluster Physics

accepted.question_text: Can the α-condensate character of α gas states be tested more broadly by calculating bosonic occupation factors, especially the occupation of the same 0S single-α orbit? In the carbon-12 Hoyle state, the benchmark is whether the three α particles occupy the same 0S orbit at a high fraction; the source reports existing Hoyle-state calculations giving about 70–80% occupation, but says that only three calculations of this quantity exist.
accepted.context_brief: Bosonic occupation factors in α gas states

evidence.quote: The α occupation numbers are a very important quantity to decide whether we have an α condensate or not. Unfortunately, very few calculations of this quantity exist.
In this respect it also would be desirable that more works attempt to calculate the bosonic occupation factors of the α’s in α gas states. So far only three results exist.

accepted.question_text: Can a direct three-α decay branch of the carbon-12 Hoyle state be experimentally observed, despite current searches only limiting the branch relative to the 8Be + α two-body decay channel to about 10^-4 without success, and can such an observation give a clearer signal of the Hoyle state's internal α structure?
accepted.context_brief: Direct three-α decay of the Hoyle state

evidence.quote: For the moment the branching ratio with the two body decay, 8Be + α, is down to 10 −4 with still no success.
However, this does not mean that the experimental e ﬀort should be stopped! It would, indeed, be very nice if a dire ct three α decay could be found.

accepted.question_text: Is the third 0+ state of carbon-12 at 10.08 MeV an excited Hoyle-family Bose condensate in which the three α particles move in relative 1S orbits, making it a higher-nodal breathing analogue of the Hoyle state, and what is the direct three-α decay behavior of such an excited condensate?
accepted.context_brief: Excited Hoyle condensate and breathing mode

evidence.quote: The 0 + 3 and 0 + 4 states at 10.08 MeV and 11.87 MeV have been identiﬁed as a brea thing mode and a bent arm excitation of the Hoyle state, respectively

One may speculate that the 0 + 3 state is a state where the three α’s move in relative 1S orbits and, thus, can be qualiﬁed to be a gain a Bose condensate, however, one with a higher nodal structure. More work has to be investigated on this exc iting aspect before ﬁrm conclusions can be reached
Th e direct three α decay out of breathing Hoyle state may be particularly interesting.

accepted.question_text: Is the first 1− state of carbon-12 an α-gas state formed by lifting one α particle from the Hoyle state into a P shell, and, if that interpretation is confirmed, how should it change the interpretation of the fifth 0+ state of oxygen-16 that has been viewed as an α particle orbiting the carbon-12 1− state?
accepted.context_brief: Carbon-12 1− α-gas state and oxygen-16 reinterpretation

evidence.quote: It , therefore, can be speculated that the 1 − state corresponds to lifting an α particle from the Hoyle state into the P-shell. Also the radi us of this 1 − state is found to be enormous. It would be very important that this new ﬁndin g of this 1 − 1 state being an α gas state be conﬁrmed.
It also may then need a re-interpretation of the 5th 0 + state in 16O which is believed to consist of an α orbiting around the 1−state in 12C, see also section 3.

accepted.question_text: Does carbon-12 really have a ground-state rotational band describable as a permanent spinning triangular α-cluster configuration, and does the proposed Hoyle band have a well-defined band head, given that mean-field calculations without projection find a round oblate shape and the transition strengths from the second 2+ state to the second and third 0+ states are similar?
accepted.context_brief: Rotational bands and spinning triangle picture in carbon-12

evidence.quote: However, there may be some caveats to this nice picture.
Never anything else than a perfectly ro und oblate shape was obtained.
So, we see, the notion of a spin ning triangle may be on not so safe grounds. Concern- ing the so-called Hoyle band also shown in Fig.5 there exist even doubts that one can call this a band at all.
So no well deﬁned band head exists.

accepted.question_text: Can ab initio descriptions of the carbon-12 Hoyle state, especially no-core Monte Carlo shell-model, symmetry-adapted no-core shell-model, and lattice QMC-EFT approaches, be validated by reproducing the Hoyle-state inelastic form factor, transition probabilities, and radius, rather than reproducing only parts of the spectrum or energy position?
accepted.context_brief: Ab initio validation of the Hoyle state

evidence.quote: So far no inelastic form factor has been calculated but the monopole t ransition probability comes out quite reasonable. Also the position is reasonably accurate. However, to be totally con vinced of the approach the inelastic form factor is needed.
However, no transition probability or inelasti c form factor have been calculated. As said above, without tho se ingredients, it is di ﬃcult to judge the value of the approach.

On the other hand neither in elastic form factor nor the transition probability have been attempted to be calculated. Even the radius, see below, completely fails since it is barely larger than the one of the ground state.
This concerns for instance the reproduction of the inelastic form factor of the Hoyle state what we think is absolutely necessary to give a ﬁnal credit to a correct theor y for the Hoyle state.

accepted.question_text: Can the sixth 0+ state of oxygen-16 near 15.1 MeV, or the experimentally observed peak near 15.2 MeV in the 20Ne + α inverse-kinematics reaction, be confirmed as the four-α Hoyle-analog gas state by measuring the inelastic form factor and assigning the spin of the 15.2 MeV state?

evidence.quote: MeV which is 700 keV above the four α threshold is suspected to be the analogue to the Hoyle state [ 40]. However, unfortunately, the inelastic form factor which is of so prec ious information for the Hoyle state has still not been measured.
a clear peak at 15.2 MeV which might be the searched for four α gas state.
It would be desirable to have the spin asi gnment of this state.
Most importantly the measurement of the inelastic form factor, w hich gives so precious information for the Hoyle state, is missing.

accepted.question_text: For the oxygen-16 candidate Hoyle-analog state, does the dilute Bose gas condense as four individual α particles or as two 8Be-like bosonic molecules, and how can those two condensation pictures be distinguished when their wave functions may strongly overlap?

evidence.quote: The decay into two 8Be is particularly interesting because 8Be is, of course also a boson and this may indicate the condens ation of two 8Be’s.

Of course, the condensation of two 8Be’s or of four α can barely be distinguished as we have already discussed for the case of the Hoyle state concerning the ∼100 % square overlap of Kamimura and THSR wave functions.
How ever, on the theoretical level the question whether a Bose gas condenses as singles or as molecules is a very interesting one [44].

accepted.question_text: Can the extended THSR description of oxygen-16 be enlarged to include negative-parity carbon-12 cluster configurations so that the missing 0+ state, described as an α particle orbiting the first 1− state of carbon-12, appears in the calculated oxygen-16 spectrum?
accepted.context_brief: Negative-parity configurations missing from THSR oxygen-16 calculations

evidence.quote: With respect to the O CM result, from the extended THSR calculation, one 0 + state is missing. This is due to the fact that, so far negative parity states are not included in the THSR scheme and then the state where an α is orbiting around the 1 − state in 12C is missing.
If the α gas nature of the 1 − 1 state in 12C is conﬁrmed, see Fig. 4, then the state state where an α orbits around this state, i.e., the 5th 0 + state, could also be an α gas state.

accepted.question_text: Which neutron-rich nuclei with valence neutrons, such as carbon-13, carbon-14, and beryllium isotopes, contain Hoyle-like α-cluster gas states, and how do extra neutrons modify the α-cluster structure relative to self-conjugate nuclei with equal neutron and proton numbers?

evidence.quote: So far, we only considered selfconjugate nuclei with N =Z. However, α clustering should survive adding some extra neutrons. For example is there some sign of a Hoyle like state in 13C or 14C, etc. ?

Further important studies concern α clustering in nuclei with valence neutrons. It is very likel y that such states exist, e.g., in 13C, 14C, etc. The works we cite show that the situation may be more co mplex as assumed.

accepted.question_text: Can a fully microscopic description of α preformation in α decay be developed for a heavy nucleus such as lead-208 plus an α particle, including the transition from an identifiable α cluster at the nuclear surface to four shell-model nucleons at higher density, and can the THSR/local-density approximation and double-folding pocket calculations be connected?
accepted.context_brief: Microscopic α preformation and α-decay pocket models

evidence.quote: The complete microscopic description of this process is very di ﬃcult. But at least the potential pocket of the α can be made visible.
A quite diﬀerent method which also produces a similar pocket has been em ployed by Adamian et al. [56]. It consists in the well known double folding procedure applied to the 212Po = 208Pb + α system.
It would be interesting to study the relation between both appr oaches.
The fully quantal description of transition of the n ucleon wave function in the α and to the shell model is very diﬃcult.
It would be interest- ing to establish a connection of the two approaches in the fut ure.
